authoredSolutions.31: Solubility of an ionic halide is decided by the balance of lattice enthalpy against hydration enthalpy. For the alkali metal fluorides the small \(F^{-}\) ion gives \(LiF\) an exceptionally large lattice enthalpy that the hydration of \(Li^{+}\) cannot compensate, so \(LiF\) is the least soluble and solubility then rises from \(LiF\) to \(CsF\). Option (A) is wrong because \(\Delta_{f}H^{\circ}\) of the alkali metal bromides becomes MORE negative down the group, and (D) is wrong for the same reason \(-\) \(LiF\) has the MOST negative \(\Delta_{f}H^{\circ}\) among the fluorides. Option (B) misdiagnoses \(CsI\): the large ions give it a LOW lattice enthalpy, and its poor solubility comes from the small hydration enthalpy of \(Cs^{+}\). Hence the correct statement is option (C).
authoredSolutions.32: Adding a limited (dilute) amount of \(NaOH\) to a \(Cr^{3 +}\) solution precipitates the grey-green hydrated chromium(III) oxide, \(Cr_{2}O_{3} \cdot nH_{2}O\), which is the form in which the so-called "chromium hydroxide" actually exists. Only with EXCESS alkali does this amphoteric precipitate redissolve as the chromite ion \(\left\lbrack Cr(OH)_{4} \right\rbrack^{-}\), so (A) is the excess-alkali product, not the dilute one. Option (C) is not a precipitate at all and carries a wrong charge for a neutral solid. Hence the answer is option (B).
authoredSolutions.33: An ester reacts with two equivalents of a Grignard reagent \(-\) the first gives a ketone through nucleophilic acyl substitution and the second adds to that ketone \(-\) so ethyl pent-4-ynoate does end up as a \(3^{\circ}\)-alcohol and Statement I is true. Statement II miscounts the equivalents: pent-4-ynoate carries a TERMINAL alkyne, whose acidic \(\equiv C-H\) destroys one mole of \(CH_{3}MgBr\) as methane before any addition occurs. The ester therefore consumes three moles of \(CH_{3}MgBr\), not two, making Statement II false. Hence option (C).
authoredSolutions.34: Stratospheric ozone is made by the Chapman cycle: high-energy ultraviolet radiation photodissociates \(O_{2}\) into oxygen atoms, \(O_{2} \xrightarrow{h\nu} O + O\), and each atom then combines with another \(O_{2}\) to give \(O_{3}\). Cosmic rays and \(\gamma\)-rays are far too scarce in the stratosphere to drive this on any useful scale, and visible light lacks the energy to break the \(O = O\) bond. Hence the formation is assisted by ultraviolet radiation, option (C).
authoredSolutions.35: Compound (A) is \(o\)-nitrophenol, whose \(OH\) is locked onto the adjacent \(NO_{2}\) group by a six-membered INTRAmolecular hydrogen bond (chelation), so it is not available for intermolecular association. Compound (C) is 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol, where the two bulky \(tert\)-butyl groups flanking the \(OH\) sterically block any approach of a second molecule. Compound (B), 4-hydroxyacetanilide, has an unhindered phenolic \(OH\) plus an amide \(N-H\) and \(C = O\), and associates strongly between molecules. Only (B) shows significant intermolecular H-bonding, which is option (A).
authoredSolutions.36: Excess acid in the stomach is triggered by histamine, the imidazole bearing a \(-CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2}\) side chain shown in option (B); it binds the \(H_{2}\) receptors of the stomach wall and stimulates secretion of \(HCl\), which is why \(H_{2}\)-blockers such as ranitidine relieve hyperacidity. Option (A) is saccharin, an artificial sweetener; option (C) is serotonin, a neurotransmitter; option (D) is phenelzine, an antidepressant. Hence the answer is option (B).
authoredSolutions.37: \(H_{2}O_{2}\) is obtained from an oxide only if that oxide is a true PEROXIDE, i.e. contains the \(O_{2}^{2 -}\) unit, which simply picks up two protons from water. \(Na_{2}O_{2}\) does this readily even at room temperature: \(Na_{2}O_{2} + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_{2}O_{2}\). \(PbO_{2}\) and \(SnO_{2}\) are dioxides, not peroxides, and merely hydrate to \(Pb(OH)_{4}\) and \(Sn(OH)_{4}\); \(BaO_{2} \cdot 8H_{2}O\) is a peroxide but needs acidification (and evaporation) rather than plain water. Hence the answer is option (B).
authoredSolutions.38: Count the carbons that survive in each route. In (A) the methyl ketone \(CH_{3}CH_{2}COCH_{3}\) undergoes the haloform reaction with \(OI^{-}\), losing the \(CH_{3}\) as \(CHI_{3}\) and leaving three carbons as propanoic acid. In (C) the \(gem\)-trihalide \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CCl_{3}\) hydrolyses at the \(CCl_{3}\) carbon to \(CH_{3}CH_{2}COOH\), again three carbons, and (B) oxidises the three-carbon chain to the same acid. Route (D), however, is a Grignard carboxylation: \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}MgBr\) adds to \(CO_{2}\) and GAINS a carbon, giving the four-carbon butanoic acid. Hence the reaction that will not yield propionic acid is option (D).
authoredSolutions.39: All five ions \(P^{3 -}, S^{2 -}, Cl^{-}, K^{+}, Ca^{2 +}\) are isoelectronic with argon, each carrying 18 electrons, so their sizes are governed only by nuclear charge. Radius therefore falls steadily as \(Z\) rises, i.e. as the \(Z/e\) ratio increases from the most negative to the most positive ion. Ordering by atomic number \(P(15) < S(16) < Cl(17) < K(19) < Ca(20)\) gives radii in the reverse order, \(P^{3 -} > S^{2 -} > Cl^{-} > K^{+} > Ca^{2 +}\), which is option (A).
authoredSolutions.40: Two equivalents of \(CH_{3}MgBr\) attack the two electrophilic sites separately. One adds to the nitrile to give a ketimine salt that hydrolyses in step (ii) to an aryl methyl ketone, converting \(-C \equiv N\) into \(-COCH_{3}\); the other adds to the ring ketone, giving a \(3^{\circ}\)-alcohol after workup. Step (iii), \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) with heat, dehydrates that \(3^{\circ}\)-alcohol, and elimination occurs toward the ring-fusion carbon because the resulting tetrasubstituted alkene is also CONJUGATED with the benzene ring, which is the more stable of the two possible alkenes. The product therefore carries an acetyl group and the endocyclic conjugated trimethyl alkene, option (A).
authoredSolutions.41: The substrate is 1-bromo-2-phenylbutane, a primary halide, but its \(\beta\)-carbon is a branched benzylic \(CH\) that shields the back side of the \(C-Br\) bond and slows \(S_{N}2\) attack by methoxide. Methoxide is also a strong base, and the only \(\beta\)-hydrogen available is the benzylic one, so E2 removal of that hydrogen produces an alkene CONJUGATED with the ring, \(CH_{3}CH_{2}C(=CH_{2})C_{6}H_{5}\) (2-phenyl-1-butene). That extra conjugation makes the elimination pathway the dominant one here, ahead of the ether that simple \(S_{N}2\) would give (option D). Option (A) would require nucleophilic substitution on an unactivated ring and (C) needs water, not methanol. Hence the major product is option (B).
authoredSolutions.42: Fluorine forms two oxides, \(OF_{2}\) and \(O_{2}F_{2}\), of which only \(OF_{2}\) is thermally stable; \(O_{2}F_{2}\) is a violently powerful fluorinating oxidant even at very low temperature. authoredSolutions.43: A lyophobic sol has no affinity for the dispersion medium, so its only defence against coagulation is the like charge carried by the particles, and adding an electrolyte destroys it at once. This solvation, not electrostatics, is why lyophilic sols are the more stable (and reversible) of the two. Hence the answer is option (D).
authoredSolutions.44: \(K_{2}CO_{3}\) deprotonates phenol to the phenoxide, which is the nucleophile in a Williamson ether synthesis with 1-bromo-3-methylbut-2-ene (prenyl bromide). authoredSolutions.46: Three of the four listed reagents are copper-based: Benedict's uses alkaline \(Cu^{2 +}\) citrate, Barfoed's uses \(Cu(CH_{3}COO)_{2}\) in acetic acid, and the Biuret test uses \(CuSO_{4}\) in alkali to give the violet peptide complex. authoredSolutions.47: Sucrose is a non-reducing disaccharide built from \(\alpha\)-D-(+)-glucose and \(\beta\)-D-(\(-\))-fructose joined head-to-head through their anomeric carbons, so hydrolysis simply releases those same two units unchanged. authoredSolutions.49: Black phosphorus exists in two forms and each has its own route. authoredSolutions.51: Use the two-temperature Arrhenius form \(\log\dfrac{k_{2}}{k_{1}} = \dfrac{E_{a}}{2.303R}\left( \dfrac{1}{T_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{T_{2}} \right)\) with \(T_{1} = 600\text{ }K\) and \(T_{2} = 700\text{ }K\). authoredSolutions.86:
Differentiate the hyperbola \(2x^{2}-y^{2}=2\) implicitly: \(4x-2y\,y'=0\), so the tangent slope at \((x_1,y_1)\) is \(y'=\dfrac{2x_1}{y_1}\) and the normal slope is \(-\dfrac{y_1}{2x_1}\).

At \(A(\sec\theta,\ 2\tan\theta)\) the normal slope is \(-\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{2\sec\theta}=-\sin\theta\). Its equation is
\[y-2\tan\theta=-\sin\theta\,(x-\sec\theta)\ \Rightarrow\ y=-x\sin\theta+\tan\theta+2\tan\theta=-x\sin\theta+3\tan\theta,\]
using \(\sin\theta\sec\theta=\tan\theta\).

Since \(\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\), we have \(\sec\phi=\csc\theta\) and \(\tan\phi=\cot\theta\). At \(B(\csc\theta,\ 2\cot\theta)\) the normal slope is \(-\cos\theta\), giving
\[y=-x\cos\theta+\cot\theta+2\cot\theta=-x\cos\theta+3\cot\theta.\]

Set the two normals equal to find the intersection:
\[-x\sin\theta+3\tan\theta=-x\cos\theta+3\cot\theta\ \Rightarrow\ x(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)=3(\cot\theta-\tan\theta)=\frac{3(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}.\]
Hence \(\alpha=x=\dfrac{3(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\).

Now
\[\beta=-\alpha\sin\theta+3\tan\theta=-\frac{3(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)}{\cos\theta}+\frac{3\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{-3\cos\theta-3\sin\theta+3\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=-3.\]

Therefore \((2\beta)^{2}=(-6)^{2}=36.\)
